text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Russian newspapers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
IZVESTIA
- Grain crops in Russia this year are expected to be about 80 million tonnes, which is higher than in 1996 and 1995, says Russia's agriculture minister.
- Tatarstan is planning to issue Eurobonds in November.
- Russia's 1998 budget assumes the government will tighten control over the way the regions spend federal budget money.
KOMMERSANT DAILY
- Russia's government is confident it can pay back all budget arrears by the end of the year.
- Fighting continues around results of the auction of Svyazivest, Russia's telecommunication giant.
- Conflict between the management of Krasnoyarsk Aluminium Smelter (KrAZ) and Rossiysky Kredit bank may be resolved soon.
- Russia may become Iraq's biggest partner in oil export.
- The State Property Committee is preparing a new privatisation model.
SEVODNYA
- The government does not seem to be disturbed by the statement of state currency and export controllers regarding legal violations during the Svyazinvest sell-off.
- Moscow's position in talks with Chechnya looks timid.
- Russia's Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin has taken a very tough line on the 1998 budget.
- Russian oil producers want to lift excise duties on oil in the new Tax Code.
NEZAVISIMAYA GAZETA
- The Kremlin is installing loyal professionals in key positions in the military, police and security structures.
ROSSIISKAYA GAZETA
- Grain crops in Russia this year are expected to be higher than last year and grain prices may fall, experts say.
- The government can no longer afford numerous social benefits to servicemen, the government paper says.
ROSSIISKIYE VESTI

- President Boris Yeltsin, apparently alarmed by a possible increase in separatist feelings among Cossacks, has suspended a decree on Cossacks' state service adopted by the local authorities in the Krasnodar region of southern Russia.
MOSKOVSKY KOMSOMOLETS
- Rouble re-denomination will not harm ordinary Russians, says the Central Bank's First Deputy Chairman Alexander Khandruyev.
-- Svetlana Kovaleva, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
